standard.title: Explore models and test relationships
standard.description: develop investigable questions, reasoned predictions and hypotheses to explore scientific models, identify patterns and test relationships
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can pose investigable questions to identify patterns and test relationships and make predictions based on experiences (AC9S5I01). They have not yet developed hypotheses with explicit variable-outcome-reasoning structure or generated questions to explore scientific models.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop investigable questions, reasoned predictions and hypotheses to explore scientific models, identify patterns and test relationships.

nodes.label: Investigable vs non-investigable questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish investigable from non-investigable questions and explain what makes a question investigable
nodes.minimum_width: Identify whether a given question is investigable or not; state at least two features that make a question investigable
nodes.typical_width: Discuss features of investigable and non-investigable questions; evaluate their own and others' questions for investigability; refine a non-investigable question into an investigable one
wider: Limited width — distinguishing investigable from non-investigable questions is a judgement skill that does not vary meaningfully across contexts. More question sets provide practice volume, not genuine breadth. Extensions such as evaluating questions from First Nations ecological knowledge contexts add cultural dimension but don't change the underlying criteria being practised.

response_modes.reason: Distinguishing investigable from non-investigable questions is a judgement skill that students commonly get wrong in both directions — either accepting untestable questions or rejecting testable ones. The concept does not vary meaningfully across contexts; what helps is repeated practice classifying and refining questions until the criteria become automatic.

Students commonly apply the label 'investigable' or 'not investigable' without being able to articulate why. Scaffolding the reasoning — what feature of this question makes it testable or untestable, and what would need to change — builds the explicit criteria that consolidation practice then reinforces.

success_criteria: Correctly classifies at least 3 questions as investigable or non-investigable
States at least two features that make a question investigable

nodes.label: Developing investigable questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop investigable questions to explore scientific models or test relationships between variables
nodes.minimum_width: Develop one investigable question to explore a model or test a relationship; identify the variables involved
nodes.typical_width: Develop investigable questions for two different purposes — one to explore a model and one to test a relationship; explain how the question connects to the model or relationship
wider: Develop investigable questions to explore scientific models such as 'How does particle theory explain the properties of substances?'
Develop investigable questions to test relationships such as 'How does the volume of a balloon change as it is heated and cooled?'
Develop multi-variable investigable questions where the relationship between variables is not immediately obvious

response_modes.reason: Students commonly write questions that are too broad ('What affects plant growth?') or too narrow ('Does water help plants?') to be genuinely investigable. Developing questions across different science contexts — models, patterns, relationships — helps students calibrate the right scope and specificity. Each new context forces fresh calibration rather than pattern-matching a single example.

Question development is not intuitive — students need an explicit reasoning scaffold: what is the model or relationship I'm exploring, what would change, and what would I measure? Without this scaffold, students produce questions that sound investigable but don't actually specify the variables or connect to the phenomenon. The scaffold is what makes breadth across contexts productive rather than just generating more poorly-formed questions.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Developing investigable questions across science contexts — particle theory, balloon volume, tidal cycles — gives advancing students practice applying the question-formation skill to increasingly complex and non-obvious relationships. The wider tier here is genuinely rich because the skill of framing a well-scoped investigable question transfers across all subsequent inquiry work.
success_criteria: Develops an investigable question that identifies variables or a model to explore
The question is testable with available methods and resources
Explains how the question connects to the model or relationship being investigated

nodes.label: Predictions and hypotheses
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can formulate reasoned predictions and hypotheses that include a variable, predicted outcome and reasoning
nodes.minimum_width: Use a provided scaffold to develop a hypothesis for a given investigation; distinguish a prediction from a hypothesis
nodes.typical_width: Formulate hypotheses independently, identifying the key elements — variable, predicted outcome, reasoning; discuss the relationship between a reasoned prediction and a hypothesis
wider: Limited width — the if...then...because hypothesis structure does not vary across investigation contexts. Formulating hypotheses for more complex investigations and evaluating student hypotheses are both practice volume on the same three-part structure, not genuinely broader contexts.

response_modes.reason: Writing well-structured hypotheses is a precision skill — students commonly omit the reasoning component or confuse predictions with hypotheses. The three-part structure (if... then... because...) does not vary across contexts; what helps is practice writing and refining hypotheses until the structure becomes fluent.

The 'because' component is what distinguishes a hypothesis from a prediction, and students consistently drop it. Explicit scaffolding of the reasoning component — why do you expect this outcome, what scientific principle or model supports it — is what makes the structure meaningful rather than a formula to fill in. Consolidation practice without structured reasoning produces fluent but hollow hypotheses.

success_criteria: Develops a hypothesis that includes a variable, predicted outcome and reasoning
Distinguishes a prediction from a hypothesis
The reasoning in the hypothesis is scientifically plausible
